thread:
Alex G.: FinServCo POC kickoff — customer wants Private deployment (VPC) with strict egress controls and TLS inspection on their side. Can we confirm recommended connectivity pattern, firewall allowlist, and any pricing/POC constraints? They want to preserve client source IP and support SNI for routing. POC target: next Wed. cc @Maria P.

Maria P.: Thanks Alex — FYI they're heavy on compliance. Main asks: static egress IPs, PrivateLink or peering advice, and impact on Dedicated vs Private pricing for traffic.

Sam K.: Quick q — are they expecting us to terminate TLS (i.e., our proxy inspects) or do they want their NGFW to inspect outbound before hitting our endpoints? That changes SNI/source-ip handling.

Alex G.: They want their NGFW to do TLS inspect (middlebox) for egress auditing. So traffic will be intercepted before reaching our infra. They still want SNI preserved to route to the right model endpoint.

Priya S. (NetOps): For Private deployment the normative pattern we recommend is interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) in the customer's VPC + our endpoint service in their account/vpc when using private mode. Options:
- A: PrivateLink (interface ENIs) in customer VPC -> our Private deploy subnets. Preserves TLS between customer app and our endpoint. If customer's NGFW does TLS inspect in front of endpoint, SNI may be removed/modified.
- B: VPC Peering with NAT egress through customer's NAT -> preserves client src IP, but peering doesn't work across accounts w/ service model as cleanly and has route table complexity.

Priya S. (NetOps): If they require static egress IPs leaving their network toward internet (for things like external integrations), they can use NAT GW or Egress-only/NAT + Elastic IPs. For traffic between their app and our PrivateLink there is no public egress.

Sam K.: Important technical notes:
- PrivateLink traffic is ENI->ENI inside AWS, no public IPs.
- If customer's NGFW sits inline before PrivateLink, TLS inspect will terminate TLS and re-initiate — SNI may be blanked or set to inspected hostname. That will break SNI-based routing on our side unless the NGFW preserves the original SNI via 'SNI passthrough' config.

Sam K.: Quick firewall snippet for them to allow traffic to our PrivateLink endpoints (customer will see regional interface endpoint IPs):
```
# Example allowlist for egress from customer app to Redwood PrivateLink (region: us-east-1)
TCP 443 -> 10.17.83.0/27   # interface endpoint ENI block (example)
TCP 443 -> 10.17.83.32/27  # interface endpoint ENI block (example)
```

Priya S. (NetOps): If they must keep TLS inspect, the recommended approach is: have the NGFW perform inspection but configure it to forward original SNI and preserve client source IP (some appliances support 'origin SNI' passthrough and X-Forwarded-For-like headers). If the appliance rewrites/removes SNI then we need an alternative routing key (e.g., client mTLS or a custom header) — that requires engineering changes.

Leah R. (Security): From a security questionnaire POV — request items:
- Confirm KMS usage for customer keys (customer-managed keys supported)
- Audit logs export (CloudTrail/Flow logs) retention options
- TLS termination boundaries: who terminates certs and where private keys live
- If NGFW inspects TLS, ensure legal/compliance acceptance for cert interception

Maria P.: Pricing note from the deal side: customer is worried PrivateLink data path may add cross-AZ or NAT egress costs. For POC can we offer credits or capped bandwidth?

Sam K.: Pricing clarity: Redwood Private license typically covers the software/platform layer; cloud egress/network bandwidth remains on customer's bill. For hosted Dedicated we charge for reserved capacity and add-ons; Private (VPC) is licensed separately. For POC we can offer limited egress credits and reduce monitoring retention to save cost — confirm with finance.

Alex G.: Customer question: If we need to change to 'proxy' pattern (our NLB terminates TLS) to preserve SNI, will that expose their traffic to Redwood termination? They want to avoid us holding plaintext.

Leah R. (Security): If we terminate TLS on our side we can mTLS between customer and our endpoints (mutual TLS) so customer controls client certs. Private keys remain on their side for client certs, but server certs are on Redwood side — acceptable if contractually agreed. We should add this as an option in the security addendum.

Priya S. (NetOps): Action items (POC):
1) Customer to share: NGFW model and TLS inspect config, desired SNI behavior, and CIDR ranges for app subnets.
2) Redwood to provide: interface endpoint IP ranges (example list), sample security group egress rules, and optional mTLS config + docs.
3) Sales/Finance to confirm POC egress credit (Maria).

Maria P.: I'll push for a 30GB egress credit for the POC and share the signed NDA. Scheduling: can we aim for infra hands-on Wed 10am PT?

Alex G.: Thanks all — I'll collect NGFW config from customer and drop into NET-4591. Will also confirm whether they can enable SNI passthrough.

Leah R. (Security): If they can't preserve SNI we'll need a follow-up design session to evaluate header-based or mTLS routing.

Sam K.: Noted. I can draft a minimal proxy/mTLS config snippet for the engineering team once we see NGFW behavior.

Maria P.: Closing loop: scheduling invite and POC access checklist will be posted in NET-4591. :thumbsup:
